conceptTag: Trader Joe's stays small on purpose
readerTitle: Why Trader Joe's chose small stores and short shelves
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Trader Joe's) + 가상 적용 (소프트웨어 회사 안의 디자인 팀)
insight: 작다는 것은 커지기 전의 단계가 아니라, 한 가지를 더 잘하기 위해 일부러 고르는 설계일 수 있다.
misconception: 상품과 서비스를 더 많이 갖출수록 고객을 더 많이 붙잡는다. 작게 머무는 것은 성장할 힘이 없다는 뜻이다.

sources.text: Coulombe, J. & Steinberg, P. (2021). Becoming Trader Joe. HarperCollins. (창업 배경, 품목 축소와 자체 브랜드 전략)
Trader Joe's, company website 'Our Story' (1967년 패서디나 첫 매장)
Kowitt, B. (2010). Inside the secret world of Trader Joe's. Fortune. (작은 매장, 적은 품목, 자체 브랜드 비중)
Inside Trader Joe's podcast (2020), 온라인 판매를 하지 않는 이유에 관한 회사 설명
Ton, Z. (2014). The Good Jobs Strategy. (적은 품목이 운영과 직원에게 주는 효과)

factChecks.note: 매장 크기와 품목 수는 정확한 숫자 대신 "일반 슈퍼마켓의 일부", "수천 개 vs 수만 개"로만 적었습니다. Fortune(2010) 등에서 자주 인용되는 수치(약 4,000개 vs 약 50,000개)는 시점과 출처마다 다르므로 넣지 않았습니다.
"대부분 자체 브랜드"라는 표현을 확인하세요. 흔히 약 80%로 인용되지만 1차 출처 확인 전이라 수치는 뺐습니다.
로열티 카드 없음, 온라인 주문·배달 없음은 게시 직전에 회사 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 정책이 바뀔 수 있어 "for years"로 적었습니다.
Trader Joe's가 1979년부터 Aldi Nord를 운영하는 Albrecht 가문 측 소유이며 비상장이라는 점은 널리 알려져 있으나, 카드에는 "privately owned"까지만 적었습니다.
1970년대 Coulombe가 품목을 줄이고 자체 브랜드를 키운 결정의 구체적 연도와 내용은 Becoming Trader Joe에서 확인하세요. 카드에는 "over the 1970s"로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Why Trader Joe's chose small stores and short shelves
body: Trader Joe's runs hundreds of grocery stores across the US. Yet each one is a fraction of the size of a typical supermarket.
It carries a few thousand products, where big supermarkets carry tens of thousands. For years it has had no loyalty card and no online ordering.
It also has one of the most loyal followings in American retail. The smallness is not an accident.

image.label: A small, cozy grocery store next to a giant supermarket
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 거대한 창고형 슈퍼마켓 옆에 아담한 동네 식료품점. 작은 가게 앞에 손님들이 즐겁게 줄 서 있음. 실제 상호, 로고, 하와이안 셔츠 등 브랜드를 연상시키는 요소는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your rivals are getting bigger.
body: You run a growing grocery chain. Supermarkets nearby are opening huge stores that stock almost everything. Some of your customers ask why you don't carry their favorite national brands.

options.text: Open bigger stores and stock the full range, so customers never need to go elsewhere
options.feedback: You remove the reason to shop elsewhere, but you also walk into the giants' game: more rent, more stock, and prices shoppers can compare line by line.

options.text: Keep stores small and the range short, mostly your own products, chosen with care
options.feedback: You lose some one-stop shoppers. In return, every shelf can be special, and nobody can compare your prices item by item. This is close to what Trader Joe's did.

options.text: Stay small, but add the top national brands customers ask for
options.feedback: It answers the requests, but each well-known brand takes shelf space and invites price comparison with bigger stores that can sell it cheaper.

cards.title: Fewer things, chosen better.
body: Joe Coulombe opened the first Trader Joe's in Pasadena, California, in 1967. Over the 1970s, he narrowed the range instead of widening it.
Products that couldn't stand out were dropped. Shelves filled up with items sold under the store's own name, often unusual ones customers couldn't find elsewhere.
The stores stayed small. Products rotated in and out. Staff were expected to know and taste what they sold.

cards.title: Smallness as a design choice
body: **Staying small on purpose** means setting limits on size or range because those limits make the business better at its one job.
Many owners treat small as a stage to grow out of. Trader Joe's treated small as the product. A short list of good things, in a store you can walk through quickly, was what customers came for.

image.label: A funnel narrowing many products down to a few chosen ones
image.brief: 깔때기 인포그래픽. 위쪽에 수많은 상품 아이콘, 아래로 내려가며 소수의 상품만 남고 각각 별표가 붙음. 아래 라벨 "Fewer items, each one chosen". 실제 브랜드 패키지 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Each limit makes another thing easier.
list: **Fewer items:** each one sells in large volume, which helps when bargaining with suppliers
**Own label:** shoppers can't compare the price with the store down the road
**Small stores:** cheaper, easier-to-find sites and less stock to manage
**Short range:** staff can actually know the products and recommend them
cards.callout: Add the full range, and every one of these gets weaker.
cards.softwareNote: A software product with a few features done very well can be easier to learn, sell and support. Every extra feature adds testing, help pages and edge cases, the digital version of shelf space.

cards.title: Small only works if the few things are special.
body: A short range costs you customers who want everything in one trip. Many Trader Joe's shoppers still visit another store for the rest.
It also demands strong product choices. Fewer, *ordinary* items is just a worse store.

And small stores are not the same as a small company. Trader Joe's grew by adding many small stores. It is also privately owned, so it hasn't faced stock-market pressure to grow each store into something bigger.

cards.title: Now it's a design team inside a company.
body: You lead a four-person design team at a mid-size software company. Every department sends requests: slides, ads, app screens, event posters. Quality is slipping and deadlines are missed.

options.text: Accept everything and ask for two more designers
options.feedback: More people may clear the queue, but the team still spreads thin across work it isn't best at, and requests tend to grow to fill the extra capacity.

options.text: Publish a short list of what the team does, such as product screens and key launches, and point other work to templates
options.feedback: Some colleagues will be unhappy at first. In return, the team gets very good at the work that matters most and can say no without arguing case by case.

options.text: Accept everything but do each job faster and simpler
options.feedback: You keep everyone happy for now, but the team becomes known for average work everywhere, which is the opposite of what it's for.

cards.title: Small can be the strategy, not the starting point.
body: Before you add more products, space or services, ask whether the limit is what makes you good.
**Try it today:** list everything your business or team offers. Mark the items you are clearly best at. What would happen if you dropped the rest?
